red_flags.title: CEQA full EIR is a 12–24+ month critical path with high litigation exposure
red_flags.evidence: A 100 MW solar+storage project on farmland in CA requires a full EIR: 12–24 months to certify, 18–30 months total entitlement, +1–3 years if litigated. Renewables are the most-frequently-challenged project type (~43% plaintiff win rate vs EIRs). Farmland impact is scored via the Agricultural LESA Model and is likely 'significant and unavoidable,' requiring a Statement of Overriding Considerations. This alone can push any COD target out by 2–3+ years.
red_flags.benchmark: CEQA EIR 12–24 months to certify; 18–30 months total entitlement; +1–3 years if litigated; ~43% plaintiff win rate

red_flags.title: OBBBA ITC beginning-of-construction cliff — deadline already passed
red_flags.evidence: Under OBBBA (July 2025) and IRS Notice 2025-42, a project with COD July 2028 receives $0 in solar ITC/PTC unless beginning-of-construction was documented by July 4, 2026 — a deadline that has already passed. No 5% safe harbor applies to >1.5 MW solar. Any permitting delay compounds this; the BOC evidence package is the single biggest go/no-go item. Storage ITC (§48E) survives the solar/wind cliff.
red_flags.benchmark: OBBBA: BOC documented by July 4, 2026 for COD July 2028; no 5% safe harbor for >1.5 MW solar

red_flags.title: Williamson Act land is an incompatible use — cancellation cost and schedule risk
red_flags.evidence: Commercial solar is an incompatible use on Williamson Act-contracted land. Exit paths: 9-year nonrenewal, or cancellation at 12.5% of unrestricted FMV (25% for Farmland Security Zone), or a solar-use easement at 6.25% (impaired farmland only). Ventura County has substantial agricultural/Williamson Act acreage; the parcel's contract status must be verified before entitlement. Cancellation adds cost and a discretionary county action that can be challenged.
red_flags.benchmark: Williamson Act cancellation at 12.5% of unrestricted FMV (25% FSA); solar-use easement 6.25% (impaired only)
sources: kb_lookup: Williamson Act incompatible use and exit paths

red_flags.title: CEC Opt-In route eligibility and mandatory CBA/prevailing-wage conditions
red_flags.evidence: The CEC Opt-In Certification (AB 205/AB 209) is the only path that preempts local zoning, but eligibility requires solar ≥50 MW AND storage ≥200 MWh. The 100 MW solar qualifies on solar, but the storage must be ≥200 MWh or the project is ineligible. The certificate requires a certified community benefits agreement plus prevailing wage and skilled-and-trained workforce. If storage <200 MWh, the project falls back to the full local entitlement + CEQA EIR path.
red_flags.benchmark: CEC Opt-In: solar ≥50 MW, storage ≥200 MWh; 270-day decision; requires certified CBA + prevailing wage + skilled-and-trained workforce

Any such modification resets study timing and would make the July 2028 COD untenable. A material-modification audit is required.
red_flags.benchmark: Material modifications that blow up queue position: POI change, MW upsize, fuel-type change, storage additions that increase service MW

findings.permitting.red_flags: CEQA full EIR critical path
contradictions.explanation: The OBBBA red flag asserts the July 4, 2026 BOC deadline 'has already passed,' anchoring the present date after July 2026. Starting the local CEQA path from that anchor: best case 18 months entitlement → ~February 2028; typical 30 months → ~February 2029; litigated (+1–3 years) → 2029–2032. Construction for 100 MW solar + BESS typically adds 12–18 months after entitlement, so local-path COD lands 2029 or later — a 1.5-to-4-year miss versus the July 2028 COD embedded in the benchmark. The only route compatible with July 2028 is CEC Opt-In: 270 days (~9 months) → decision ~May 2027, plus 12–18 months construction → mid/late 2028, and that route is gated on storage ≥200 MWh, which is nowhere stated. Note: the July 2028 COD itself appears only inside a benchmark assumption — no extracted fact corroborates it (facts array is empty), so this contradiction is conditional on that assumption being the real project target.

claims: CAISO benchmark: IR→COD ~5 years; only ~20% of queued projects reach COD
sources: findings.permitting.benchmarks: CAISO IR→COD ~5 years, ~20% reach COD
contradictions.explanation: Ventura is in CAISO/SCE territory. If the project does not already hold an executed interconnection agreement (status unknown — no extracted facts), then from the post-July-2026 anchor implied by the OBBBA flag, 5 years IR→COD lands ~2031, roughly 3 years past the July 2028 target. July 2028 is only achievable if the project is already deep in the cluster-study process with network-upgrade costs known; nothing in the fact set establishes queue position. This compounds the CEQA contradiction: both the entitlement clock and the interconnection clock independently exceed the assumed COD.

sources: findings.permitting.red_flags: CEQA full EIR critical path
contradictions.explanation: The two flags rest on mutually exclusive routing assumptions, and the single datum that decides between them — storage capacity in MWh versus the ≥200 MWh Opt-In threshold — is absent from every fact set (site_specifics state only '100 MW solar + storage'; facts array is empty). The solar leg qualifies (100 MW ≥ 50 MW), so eligibility pivots entirely on the unstated MWh. Until that number is produced, the critical-path schedule (and therefore the COD feasibility finding) cannot be resolved: the two paths differ by roughly 9–21+ months (270 days vs 18–30 months).

claims: OBBBA red flag: the July 4, 2026 beginning-of-construction deadline 'has already passed'
No extracted fact establishes the current date, any document date, or the existence/absence of a BOC evidence package (facts array is empty)
contradictions.explanation: The most consequential assertion in the findings — that the solar ITC is already dead because July 4, 2026 has passed — is a temporal claim with no date anchor in the extracted record. There are no document dates (no PPA, no IA, no application filings, no BOC documentation) to confirm either the current date or whether beginning-of-construction was in fact documented before the deadline. If a valid BOC package exists (physical-work test; the 5% safe harbor is unavailable for >1.5 MW solar), the 'deadline passed' framing is moot; if none exists, the project's solar ITC/PTC is $0 and any financial model assuming it is wrong. The flag's conclusion may be correct, but it is unverifiable against an empty fact set.

Provide the beginning-of-construction (BOC) evidence package and continuity records to verify ITC/PTC eligibility under the OBBBA (physical-work test; no 5% safe harbor for >1.5 MW solar).
Provide the CAISO queue position, cluster study phase, and estimated network upgrade costs.
Provide site control evidence (title, lease, option) and total acreage.
Provide Williamson Act contract status and any exit path analysis (9-year nonrenewal, cancellation, or solar-use easement).
Provide equipment procurement status, especially GSU/large power transformer orders and contractually confirmed delivery dates.
Provide the actual COD target and current entitlement status (application filed, EIR underway, CEC Opt-In filing).
Provide the current date anchor and any document dates to verify the timeline (e.g., PPA, IA, application filings).
Provide the Ventura County zoning designation and any solar/BESS-specific ordinance applicability.
Provide PPA or contracted MW data and counterparty details.
Provide AB 52 tribal consultation status and NAHC Sacred Lands File check results.
Provide permit status for SWPPP/CGP, CDFW 1602, grading/building, and NFPA 855/UL 9540A fire marshal sign-off.
Provide CAPEX and cost data to cross-check against materials/equipment indices.
